title: How the PRITHVI AI risk index works
text: The risk index is a relative score from 0 to 100 calculated for every 100 m analysis zone. It combines four factors that are each normalised to a 0 to 1 range: terrain susceptibility, the rainfall scenario, drainage vulnerability and exposure.

title: How the PRITHVI AI risk index works
text: The provisional weights are 0.30 for terrain, 0.25 for rainfall, 0.25 for drainage and 0.20 for exposure. These weights are design assumptions chosen for the prototype. They are not calibrated against historical flood events.

title: How the PRITHVI AI risk index works
text: When the flood simulation for a scenario finishes, the score switches from provisional to final. The final index adds a simulated water factor W, which measures how much water the scenario's own flood run put into the zone. The final weights are 0.45 for simulated water, 0.20 for terrain, 0.15 for drainage and 0.20 for exposure. Rainfall drops out of the final formula because it is the same in every zone and reaches the score through the simulated water instead. This keeps the zone colours consistent with the 3D water: a zone that stays dry in the simulation cannot reach the highest band. Consistency is not accuracy; the simulation itself is uncalibrated.

title: How the PRITHVI AI risk index works
text: The index is not a flood probability and not a flood depth. It only ranks zones relative to each other under the selected assumptions. A higher index means the terrain, rainfall input, drainage assumption and mapped assets together make the zone a stronger candidate for attention.

title: How the PRITHVI AI risk index works
text: Display bands are Lower (below 35), Moderate (35 to 48), Higher (48 to 60) and Highest relative index (60 and above). The band thresholds are display choices, not hazard thresholds.

title: What the drainage blockage setting means
text: No surveyed drainage inventory was available for the pilot area. The storm-drain inlets shown in the twin are proxy points spread evenly along drivable roads. They do not show where real drains are.

title: What the drainage blockage setting means
text: The blockage slider marks a chosen share of those proxy inlets as unavailable, always the same inlets in the same order so results are repeatable. You can also click an individual inlet in the 3D view to block or clear it.

title: What the drainage blockage setting means
text: Blocking inlets raises the drainage vulnerability factor of nearby zones and removes drainage capacity from the water simulation. This is a sensitivity assumption. It is not an inspection record and does not claim that any real drain is blocked.

title: What the 3D water simulation is and is not
text: The 3D water surface comes from a simplified two-dimensional shallow-water solver on a 12.5 m grid. Rain falls according to a symmetric triangular hyetograph that rises to a peak at the midpoint of the chosen duration and then falls to zero. Water flows downhill around building footprints, collects in low ground and leaves through proxy inlets, optional temporary pumps and an assumed downstream outfall.

title: What the 3D water simulation is and is not
text: The solver is uncalibrated. The terrain comes from a coarse 90 m surface model with depression filling, road cells are assumed to sit 0.15 m lower than their surroundings, and runoff coefficients are assumptions. Depths are scenario outputs for comparison only. They are not forecasts and must not be read as street-level flood depth.

title: What the 3D water simulation is and is not
text: Vertical exaggeration of 3 times is applied in the 3D view so that relief and shallow water are visible.

title: What the 3D water simulation is and is not
text: After the rain stops, standing water is assumed to recede with a time constant of about one hour. This stands for drainage the model cannot resolve, such as gaps and gutters, infiltration and evaporation, and it is an assumption rather than a measurement. Peak depths and peak flooded areas are not affected by it.

title: Data sources used by the pilot
text: Buildings, roads, facilities and water bodies come from OpenStreetMap contributors through the Overpass API under the ODbL licence. OpenStreetMap coverage varies, so the pilot area is probably under-mapped, and many buildings use a proxy height of two to four storeys.

title: Data sources used by the pilot
text: Terrain comes from the Copernicus GLO-90 digital surface model sampled through the Open-Meteo elevation service at roughly 90 m posting. It is smoothed, resampled to 12.5 m and depression-filled. It cannot resolve kerbs, culverts or underpasses.

title: Data sources used by the pilot
text: Rainfall is always a user-defined scenario. NASA GPM IMERG is listed as a future calibration source, but its native resolution is far coarser than street level.

title: Data sources used by the pilot
text: Every layer is labelled observed, derived, proxy or simulated in the Data and limits tab.

title: Where to find official forecasts and warnings
text: PRITHVI AI is not an official source. For real weather warnings use the India Meteorological Department at mausam.imd.gov.in. For national disaster-management guidance use the National Disaster Management Authority at ndma.gov.in. For river and reservoir information use the Central Water Commission at cwc.gov.in. For local alerts, shelters and emergency instructions follow your district administration and state disaster management authority.

title: Where to find official forecasts and warnings
text: In an emergency contact the official emergency services. Do not rely on this prototype for decisions about safety, travel or evacuation.

title: General flood preparedness checklist (demo summary)
publisher: PRITHVI AI team summary of widely published flood-safety practice
text: This is a short demo summary of commonly published flood-preparedness practice. It is not an official document. Verify against current guidance from your disaster management authority before relying on it.

title: General flood preparedness checklist (demo summary)
publisher: PRITHVI AI team summary of widely published flood-safety practice
text: Before heavy rain: know your local shelter locations and the official alert channels. Keep a small emergency kit with drinking water, medicines, a torch, a charged phone and important documents in a waterproof bag. Move valuables and electrical items above ground level where possible.

title: General flood preparedness checklist (demo summary)
publisher: PRITHVI AI team summary of widely published flood-safety practice
text: During flooding: follow instructions from local authorities. Avoid walking or driving through floodwater because depth, currents and hidden hazards are hard to judge. Keep away from fallen power lines and switch off electricity at the mains only if it is safe to reach the switch.

title: General flood preparedness checklist (demo summary)
publisher: PRITHVI AI team summary of widely published flood-safety practice
text: After flooding: avoid contact with floodwater, which can be contaminated. Do not return to flooded buildings until authorities say it is safe.

title: Reading the facilities and road-exposure results
text: Facilities shown are those mapped in OpenStreetMap: hospitals and clinics, fire and police stations, and schools or places of worship that could be shelter candidates. Their capacity, current status and suitability as shelter are unknown to the prototype.

title: Reading the facilities and road-exposure results
text: A facility or road segment is listed as exposed when it lies inside a zone in the Higher or Highest index band under the current scenario. That is an overlay of mapped assets on indicative zones. It does not mean the asset is flooded or unusable.

title: Reading the facilities and road-exposure results
text: The road route analysis removes road segments whose simulated peak water depth exceeds a threshold you choose, then looks for the shortest remaining path between two facilities. It is a graph-based scenario analysis. It is not a certified safe route and must not be used for navigation or dispatch.

title: How inspection priority is ranked
text: The priority list ranks zones by the scenario risk index weighted by exposure, with a small bonus for zones containing mapped critical facilities. The result is a suggestion for where planners might look first, for example to inspect drainage or pre-position resources.

title: How inspection priority is ranked
text: It is not an instruction to evacuate, a dispatch order or a statement that any location is safe. Each entry shows the main driver of its score so that a person can judge whether the reasoning makes sense.

title: Live mode and forecast-driven scenarios
text: Live mode drives the scenario from the real hourly rain forecast for the next 24, 48 or 72 hours instead of the rain sliders. The forecast is the ECMWF IFS 0.25 degree ensemble from the Open-Meteo Ensemble API, which has 51 members.

title: Live mode and forecast-driven scenarios
text: Live mode is a forecast-driven planning scenario. It is not an official forecast and not a flood warning. Official weather and flood warnings come from the India Meteorological Department, NDMA and the district administration.

title: Live mode and forecast-driven scenarios
text: The low, likely and high cases are the ensemble members at the 10th, 50th and 90th percentile of total rain over the chosen window. Whole members are used so that each case is a storm shape the model actually produced. The panel also shows the full range of rain across all members.

title: Live mode and forecast-driven scenarios
text: The forecast grid is about 25 km, so the whole pilot area sits inside one grid cell and the forecast rain is the same everywhere in it. Thunderstorm timing and location are uncertain. The flood model underneath is still uncalibrated, so Live mode shows what a forecast could mean for the streets, not what will happen.

title: How PRITHVI AI is checked against real flooding
text: The Replay tab replays a past day's storm through the flood model and compares the result with waterlogging that was actually reported, such as news reports with a location. This is the project's check of accuracy against the real world, separate from its internal consistency tests.

title: How PRITHVI AI is checked against real flooding
text: For a chosen date, PRITHVI loads two rain series: the forecast issued the day before, from the Open-Meteo Previous Runs archive (available from January 2024), and the rain that fell, from the ECMWF and ERA5 reanalysis archive. Both are model products, not rain-gauge records.

title: How PRITHVI AI is checked against real flooding
text: A reported spot counts as a hit if a zone flagged Higher or Highest by the final score lies within 150 metres of it. Flagged zones with no report nearby are not called false alarms, because a missing news report does not mean there was no flooding.

title: How PRITHVI AI is checked against real flooding
text: The team chooses the event and collects the reports before looking at the model output, and reports the result whatever it shows. How accurate is PRITHVI AI? The honest answer is the hit rate from these replays. Until replays are recorded in docs/validation.md, no accuracy figure is claimed.
